title: Special Products and Factorisation — Class 10 NIOS Mathematics
subject: Mathematics

slides.title: Special Products and Factorisation
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. Today we meet five identities worth memorising — and learn to read them in BOTH directions: expand a product, or factor a polynomial.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Apply (a ± b)^2 and (a + b)(a − b) fluently.
Use (x + a)(x + b) to expand and to factor.
Expand (a ± b)^3; factor sum / difference of cubes.
Pull out the common factor from any polynomial.
Factor quadratics — by find-the-pair (a = 1) or by splitting the middle term.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective; ask students which they feel least sure about.

slides.title: Square of a binomial
bullets: Same shape; only the middle SIGN changes.
RHS is called a perfect-square trinomial.
Common slip: dropping the middle 2ab term.
slides.speaker_notes: Derive both via FOIL. Stress: middle term ≠ 0 in general.

slides.title: Difference of squares & product-sum
bullets: (a + b)(a − b) = a^2 − b^2 — middle terms cancel.
Coefficient of x is the SUM; constant is the PRODUCT.
Reverse direction: factor x^2 + bx + c by find-the-pair.
slides.speaker_notes: Use 103 × 97 to show the mental-arithmetic power; verify on board.

slides.title: Cubes — expansions
bullets: Four terms; signs alternate in (a − b)^3.
Derivation: (a + b)·(a + b)^2 — square first, multiply once more.
slides.speaker_notes: Optional: derive (a + b)^3 live by writing (a + b)·(a^2 + 2ab + b^2).

slides.title: Cubes — factor identities
bullets: Note: middle term sign of QUADRATIC factor is OPPOSITE to that of (a ± b).
slides.speaker_notes: Students often confuse the inner sign of the quadratic factor — drill on this.

slides.title: Factorisation step 1 — common factor
bullets: Always pull out the GCF first.
GCF includes BOTH numerical and variable parts.
Even when the common factor is itself a binomial: (x − 1)·(...).
slides.speaker_notes: Make explicit that (x − 1) can be a 'common factor' too — not just monomials.

slides.title: Factorisation step 2 — regrouping
bullets: Use when no factor is common to all terms.
Pair terms so each pair pulls out a matching binomial factor.
slides.speaker_notes: If the first pairing doesn't work, try a different one — there's no formula, just experimentation.

slides.title: Find-the-pair (a = 1): factor x^2 − 7x + 12
bullets: Need p + q = −7 and p · q = 12.
slides.speaker_notes: Make the SIGN-PATTERN explicit: sum, product → both negative.

slides.title: Splitting the middle term: 3x^2 + 11x + 6
bullets: Need two numbers with sum 11 and product 18.
slides.speaker_notes: Drill the four steps: a·c, find pair, split, regroup.

slides.title: Recognising patterns in factorisation
bullets: Strategy order: GCF → pattern → split-the-middle → regroup.
slides.speaker_notes: The 'strategy order' is the deliverable students should write in their notebooks.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room. Common slips: forgetting 2ab middle term; missing a sign in split-the-middle; forgetting to combine like terms.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q3. To factor 6x^2 + 7x − 3, what is a·c?
Q4. Is x^2 + 4 a difference of squares?
slides.speaker_notes: Address the question with the most disagreement.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: (a ± b)^2, (a + b)(a − b), (x + a)(x + b), (a ± b)^3, a^3 ± b^3 — five identities to memorise.
Same identities work in both directions: expand AND factor.
Factorisation order: GCF → special-product pattern → split-the-middle → regroup.
Factorisation reveals zeros — bridge to the next chapter.
slides.speaker_notes: Hand out the worksheet and announce homework.
